analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal income, payroll, and estate taxes and replaces them with a national sales tax.
analysis.headline: The Fair Tax Act of 2007, which would have replaced income, payroll, and estate taxes with a national retail sales tax, drew 72 cosponsors but never got a committee hearing or a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. John Linder's Fair Tax Act of 2007 would have abolished the federal income tax, the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare, and the estate and gift tax [S2][S3]. In their place, it would have levied a national tax on everything consumers buy. The plan included a monthly "prebate" — a cash rebate sent to every household to cover the tax on spending up to the poverty level — so that people living at subsistence would effectively pay no federal tax, and states would administer the tax collection and be compensated for the administrative costs [S3]. Supporters said this would make taxation simpler and more transparent. But a consumption tax replaces a system where tax rates rise with income — including tax on capital gains, dividends, and large inheritances — with one where everyone pays the same rate at the register. Households that spend nearly all of their wages would pay tax on almost every dollar they earn, while households living off investments and inherited wealth would largely stop paying federal tax on those gains. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 4, 2007 and never received any further action — no markup, no hearing on the record shown, no floor vote — before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would have been high-wealth households and investors: the income tax on capital gains, dividends, and interest, plus the estate and gift tax, would have been repealed entirely [S2], while a flat tax on consumption would fall hardest on wage earners who spend most of their pay. Retailers and state tax agencies would also have gained — retailers would collect the federal tax and be paid an administrative fee, and states would receive federal compensation for running the collection system [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, employment (payroll) tax, and estate and gift tax, ending individual income tax filing and the tax on large inheritances.

Replaces those taxes with a single national tax on retail sales, with a monthly rebate ("prebate") to every household covering the tax on spending up to the poverty level, so that the poorest households would pay no net federal tax.
Delegates collection to existing state sales tax systems and pays states for administrative costs, so taxpayers would deal with state agencies rather than a new federal tax bureaucracy.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on households that spend most of what they earn — wage earners, renters, and retirees drawing down savings — who would pay the national sales tax on nearly every purchase. Households with large incomes from investments and inherited estates would see those income sources go untaxed. Honest supporters of the plan acknowledge that the middle of the income distribution would likely pay a larger share of total taxes than under the current income tax, offset only in part by the monthly prebate; critics also note that if revenue targets missed, the sales tax rate would have to rise.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners who spend most of their income

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection: a flat tax on consumption shifts the burden away from income from wealth — capital gains, dividends, and inheritances would go untaxed [S2] — and toward wages, since a wage earner who spends nearly all their pay is taxed on effectively all of it while a wealthy household spending a small share of its wealth pays far less.

The monthly prebate protects households at the poverty level, but families in the middle of the income distribution would pay the full sales tax rate on purchases with no offset beyond the rebate, and an honest supporter would concede that if collections fell short of current revenue, the tax rate would have to go up.

The transition itself is disruptive: prices, paychecks, and contracts written under the income tax would all have to be renegotiated, and state governments would take on the compliance burden of collecting a federal tax [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefits are real: no income tax filing, no tax on savings until spent, and a rebate that untaxes subsistence spending. But weighed against those benefits is a structural shift of the tax burden from wealth to wages — the repeal of the estate tax and the elimination of tax on investment income overwhelmingly favor the wealthiest households, while middle-income wage earners would pay tax on a larger share of their earnings than they do today. The plan was candid about one thing its supporters rarely emphasize: the tax is added to the price of everything people buy, which the bill itself described as a risk of hiding the true cost of government in prices [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 4, 2007 and sat there for the entire two-year Congress — no markup, no hearing, no floor vote — and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Fair Tax Act of 2007 was introduced on January 4, 2007 by Rep. John Linder and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.

Seventy-two members of the House cosponsored the bill — 71 Republicans and 1 Democrat — but the Democratic-led Ways and Means Committee took no further action on it for the rest of the 110th Congress.
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing progressive income tax system stayed in place, so households that would have paid more under a national consumption tax — wage earners and middle-income families — were spared the shift. The tax-preparation and estate-planning industries, which sell services that the FairTax would have made unnecessary, also kept their market. Nobody gained dramatically; the bill simply never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners kept the income tax system

for.name: Rep. John Linder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2007 on the first day of the 110th Congress and served as its chief sponsor.

for.name: 71 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the most cosponsored tax bills of the Congress without producing any committee action.

for.name: 1 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Was the only Democratic member to cosponsor the bill.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill during the entire 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 71 of the bill's 72 cosponsors were Republicans, the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on it, and no vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the income tax on capital gains, dividends, and interest, and repealed the estate and gift tax [S2], while replacing a progressive income tax with a flat tax on consumption that falls hardest on wage earners.

industries.industry: State tax administrations and retail collection
industries.note: The bill delegates collection of the federal tax to state sales tax systems and pays states for administrative costs [S3], locking in state agencies and retailers as the permanent collection channel.
Retailers would have collected the federal sales tax and received an administrative fee for doing so [S3], while corporate income tax would be repealed [S2].

Repealing the income tax, employment tax, and estate and gift tax [S2] would have eliminated the filing and estate-planning work these industries sell; their interest lay in keeping the current system.
